paragraphs.heading: What the equation describes
paragraphs.text: The Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, also called the classical or ideal rocket equation, is a piece of mathematics about how rockets move. Here a rocket means any device that speeds itself up by throwing part of its own mass out at high speed. It can move this way thanks to the conservation of momentum. The equation packs the core physics of rocket flight into one short line.

paragraphs.heading: Four people, one result
paragraphs.text: The equation carries the name of the Russian scientist Konstantin Tsiolkovsky, who worked it out and published it in 1903. The British mathematician William Moore had already derived it in 1810 and put it in a book in 1813. The American Robert Goddard reached it in 1912 while working on better rocket engines for possible spaceflight, and the German engineer Hermann Oberth reached it around 1920 while asking whether space travel was feasible. All four got there on their own. Tsiolkovsky is honored as the first to use it to ask whether rockets could ever go fast enough for space travel.

paragraphs.heading: The three quantities
paragraphs.text: The equation links three things. The first is m₀, the starting mass including every bit of propellant. The second is m_f, the final mass once the propellant is gone, also called the dry mass. The third is vₑ, the speed of the exhaust measured relative to the rocket. The change in speed depends on that exhaust speed and on the ratio m₀/m_f, and one way to write it is m_f = m₀e^(−ΔV/vₑ). The difference m₀ − m_f is the mass of propellant used up.

paragraphs.heading: What delta-v means
paragraphs.text: The speed change in the equation is called delta-v, written Δv and said "delta-vee". In spaceflight it measures the impulse a maneuver needs, such as launching from a planet, landing on a moon or changing orbit. It is measured in units of speed. In empty space, firing along the direction of travel raises the speed by that amount, and firing the opposite way lowers it. Gravity and drag also act on a real vehicle, so delta-v is not always its actual change in speed.

paragraphs.heading: The tyranny of the rocket equation
paragraphs.text: The equation has a harsh consequence. The starting mass with propellant on board has to grow exponentially as the delta-v you want goes up. More propellant makes the rocket heavier, and a heavier rocket burns more fuel, so there is a ceiling on how much payload it can carry. This has been called the tyranny of the rocket equation. A related measure in aerospace engineering is the propellant mass fraction: the share of the starting mass that is burned along the way and never reaches the destination. It is usually used to judge how well a vehicle performs.

paragraphs.heading: Where it stops working
paragraphs.text: The equation counts only the push from the rocket engine. It leaves out other forces such as air resistance and gravity, so for a launch from a planet with an atmosphere those effects must be added to the delta-v needed. It still works for any rocket-like vehicle whose effective exhaust speed stays constant. It does not cover ways of moving that are not rockets at all, such as aerobraking, gun launches, space elevators, tethers or light sails.
